UQ Gatton trials cancer drug that could cure dogs with terminal tumours
Date: Mon Feb  9 01:00:00 2026 UTC

UQ Gatton Professor Rachel Allavena said the drug Enzistat developed by American pharmaceutical company Avammune has the potential to treat cancers in dogs and humans. "It gives dogs in southeast Queensland another option, and it's always nice to do cutting edge trials," she said. "The early data that the company has is that it's helped dogs survive longer and have less bad side effects from their cancer. "We're quite hopeful that for dogs that might not have a lot of options that it might be a useful drug in the future." UQ is looking for 30 dogs with inoperable tumours and 30 dogs in palliative care to be part of the trial. Professor Allavena said they hope the drug can shrink inoperable tumours so they could be removed surgically and give a final hope for dogs in palliative care. "They don't have hope for a cure any other way, but their owners just want to see if they can keep them to be around a little longer and see if it can make them more comfortable," she said. She said a third to a half of dogs will get cancer and it is more common than in lots of other species. Professor Allavena has been researching immune-based cancer therapies for about 15 years and she said it was really hard at times. "It's really hard when we hear about one of our patients passing away," she said. "We do also get a lot of joy from giving people hope or giving the animals options." Anyone interested in joining the trial need a cancer diagnosis and referral from their vet. People involved in the trial would need to give a tablet to their dog twice a day for six weeks and need to come to UQ Gatton three times throughout the trial. The medication and any additional blood tests, biopsies, or examinations are provided as part of the study and owners have to cover any other veterinary costs. Contact uqvets.sa@uq.edu.au to join the trial.

Cats could help scientists better understand human cancer, study says (https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/2026/05/30/scientists-find-cancer-gene-similarities-cats-humans-study-says/)
【turn1039news30】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 4 months ago; A recent study led by Louise van der Weyden and international researchers has discovered significant genetic similarities between feline and human cancers, offering promising avenues for shared treatment advancements. Analyzing tumor samples from nearly 500 domestic cats across multiple countries, the researchers identified common mutations in about 1,000 cat genes that correspond to human cancer genes. Among the most striking parallels was the FBXW7 gene, a tumor suppressor found mutated in both feline mammary tumors and human breast cancer, associated with poor prognoses.

Published in the journal Science, the research underlines cats as effective disease models due to their genetic closeness to humans and shared living environments that expose them to similar carcinogens. The study also revealed chemotherapy drug vincristine’s effectiveness in treating feline mammary tumors, providing a potential pathway for clinical trials and the development of targeted treatments. While experts like Jaime Modiano stress that more research is needed, the findings mark a significant step toward dual-species cancer therapy, benefiting both feline and human patients.
Cancer progresses faster in dogs than in people, meaning researchers can receive quicker results with potential treatments in clinical trials with canines. The bone cancer osteosarcoma is more common in dogs than people, so scientists have learned techniques from the animals on how to treat people with the same cancer, and vice versa.
A decade ago, researchers told The Washington Post that dogs were observed more than cats in oncology studies because less was known about feline tumors and cats tended to become more stressed interacting with people.
For their study, van der Weyden and other researchers collected tissue samples from domestic cats from Austria, Canada, England, Germany, New Zealand and Scotland. 
They screened about 1,000 cat genes that are equivalent to human genes associated with cancer. Van der Weyden said she worried they might not find similarities between cat and human cancers, partly because few cat genetic studies had been completed. 
However, in addition to the gene associated with breast cancer in both species, researchers said they found similarities in human and cat cancers affecting their blood, bones, lungs, skin, gastrointestinal tract and central nervous system.
"I was first of all doing it for the cat," said van der Weyden, senior staff scientist at the Wellcome Sanger Institute, a genomics research center in Cambridgeshire, England. "But then to find that there are similarities and we can help humans, that's fantastic."
Researchers found that the chemotherapy drug vincristine was effective against cats' mammary tumors, according to the study, which was published in February. They said that finding could guide veterinary pharmaceutical companies in developing treatment for mammary cancer, which is the third-most-common feline cancer and is typically deadly, according to Cornell University's Feline Health Center.
"Before we just didn't know; we didn't know what drug you could potentially pick," said Wood, who teaches pathology at the University of Guelph in Ontario. "And now there's sort of a list, at least, that could then proceed to clinical trials."
Jaime Modiano, a professor at the University of Minnesota's school of veterinary medicine who was not involved in the research, said the study is a foundation for scientists to learn more about cat and human cancers. However, he said, much more research is required to determine whether the findings can lead to treatments for cats - let alone helping with human cancers.
"It's the first step," Modiano said, "in the journey of a thousand miles."

【turn1039news31】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 1.1 years ago; A new study, published by researchers from UCSF, UC Davis, and the University of Pittsburgh, presents a groundbreaking cancer treatment for cats that may also benefit human patients with head and neck tumors. The therapy targets STAT3, a transcription factor known to be hyperactivated in about 75% of human tumors. Researchers created a DNA-based decoy molecule that inhibits STAT3 by mimicking the genetic sequences it typically binds to, thereby preventing it from triggering cancer-promoting genes.

In a clinical trial involving 20 pet cats with oral cancer, 35% showed tumor shrinkage or stability, with minimal side effects. One cat, Jak, significantly outlived his prognosis, benefiting from the therapy. The decoy treatment was administered intravenously, an improvement over previous versions requiring direct tumor injection.

The findings revealed immune system changes in treated cats, offering potential biomarkers for identifying patients—both feline and human—who may benefit most. With promising results and improved survival rates in responsive cats, researchers are aiming to fund early-phase human trials while continuing feline studies, suggesting possible future cross-species cancer therapies.
A new cancer treatment for cats could help humans, too
Date: Thu Aug 28 15:00:17 2025 UTC

In a study published Thursday, scientists from UCSF, UC Davis and the University of Pittsburgh describe a promising, first of its kind treatment in pet cats with oral cancer. The authors say the approach could benefit people with head and neck tumors, too.
"There are common features of cancer in cats and cancer in humans," said author Jennifer Grandis, a professor in UCSF's Department of Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery. "We can learn from each other."
The new treatment targets the STAT3 transcription factor, a protein that binds specific DNA sequences to affect gene expression. "This transcription factor is hyperactivated in almost three-quarters of human tumors," said author Daniel Johnson, a professor in UCSF's Department of Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery.
Until now, the protein has proven "incredibly difficult to inhibit," Johnson said. "People have been trying to develop drugs against this protein, STAT3, for many years.

Determined to save her, Conyngham used ChatGPT and AI data processing to analyze Rosie's genomic data, identify cancer mutations, and design a personalized mRNA vaccine with help from experts at the University of NSW.

Rosie's improved health underscores the promise of mRNA technology in personalized cancer care, both for animals and potentially humans. Rescue dog Rosie’s cancer shrinks after world-first mRNA vaccine
Date: Fri Mar 13 09:30:00 2026 UTC

Now the hi-tech teamwork has unleashed an experimental medicine that offers hope to human patients, by using mRNA vaccines in oncology. Abandoned in bushland, eight-year-old Rosie found her forever home with Sydney tech entrepreneur Paul Conyngham, who adopted the staffy-shar pei cross from an animal shelter in 2019 - just in time for pandemic lockdowns. Heartbroken when his fur-baby was diagnosed with a deadly mast cell cancer in 2024, Mr ­Conyngham threw thousands of dollars at veterinary chemotherapy and surgery, which slowed but failed to shrink the tumours. Now, after treatment with a custom mRNA cancer vaccine over the Christmas break, the tennis ball-sized tumour on Rosie's hock has shrunk in half, in a recovery that has astounded researchers at the cutting-edge of human cancer treatments. "It was like holy crap, it worked!'' says Martin Smith, an associate professor of computational biology and director of the Ramaciotti Centre for Genomics at the University of NSW.

Yale-developed canine cancer vaccine shows promise for dogs, doubling survival rates (https://www.nhregister.com/news/article/ct-yale-dogs-canine-cancer-vaccine-mamula-therapy-20804986.php)
【turn1039news33】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 1.2 years ago; A promising canine cancer vaccine developed by Dr. Mark Mamula and his team at the Yale School of Medicine is showing significant success in extending the lives of dogs diagnosed with aggressive cancers like osteosarcoma. The vaccine, currently in clinical trials conducted by Mamula’s company TheraJan, targets protein families such as EGFR/HER2, which are responsible for tumor growth. By blocking these proteins and initiating a strong immune response that kills tumors, the vaccine has doubled 12-month survival rates when combined with standard treatments like surgery and chemotherapy—from 30–40% to 60–70%.

The vaccine gained attention following the remarkable recovery of Ranger, a golden retriever previously given little chance of survival. After receiving the vaccine, his cancer ceased progressing and disappeared from scans. Over 11 clinical trial sites across the U.S. are offering the treatment, free of charge, to eligible dogs. The vaccine is pending approval from the USDA and is expected to become the most affordable cancer treatment for dogs on the market. Given the prevalence of cancer in dogs—affecting one in four and half of those over age 10—the vaccine could have far-reaching impact. Mamula, inspired by the loss of his own dog, continues to receive grateful messages from pet owners whose dogs have benefited.
Yale-developed canine cancer vaccine shows promise for dogs, doubling survival rates
Date: Fri Aug  8 09:00:19 2025 UTC

NEW HAVEN - The owner of a 7-year-old golden retriever with an aggressive form of cancer was out of options.
Rick Kneisel, who lives alone in a small city south of Dayton, Ohio, first noticed an issue with his dog, Ranger, in March 2019. A noticeable limp that he initially thought was a pulled muscle turned out to be osteosarcoma, a common and fast-spreading bone cancer in dogs. For Kneisel, 75, the news was "devastating."
Ranger had one of his front legs amputated and endured months of treatment, including chemotherapy and an experimental drug from Ohio State University. But his condition worsened, Kneisel said. The cancer had spread to Ranger's lungs and his chances of survival were dimming.
That's when Kneisel called Dr. Mark Mamula, an immunologist and professor at the Yale School of Medicine, who, along with a team of researchers, were developing a canine cancer vaccine that's now changing the outlook for dogs with cancer and offering hope to their owners.
"You start doing the numbers with 90 million dogs, there are large populations of dogs in this country that are destined to get cancers," Mamula said
Mamula's quest for a canine cancer treatment was motivated by a personal loss. About a dozen years ago, his 10-year-old golden retriever, Savannah, died of hemangiosarcoma, an aggressive form of cancer in dogs that arises from blood vessels, according to PetMD. 
"I realized at the time that the tools the veterinarian oncologists have at their disposal were just not what one can find in treating human cancers by comparison," he said.
In search of a solution, he teamed up with Gerald Post, then a Norwalk-based veterinarian oncologist, in 2015. Together, the two launched an early-phase study for a novel cancer vaccine - work that Mamula said "paved the way" for the clinical trials now underway, although Post is no longer involved in the research.
Since the initial study, Mamula and his team have gained a better understanding of which dog breeds and cancer types the vaccine might treat most effectively, allowing them to refine their approach.
Mamula called his cancer vaccine research "the most satisfying work that I've done" in his more than 35 years at Yale. He often gets emails from dog owners a year or two - sometimes even three - after their pets receive immunotherapy, sharing updates on their post-cancer lives.
But the messages that resonate most, he said, come from older, usually widowed owners whose dogs are beloved companions or service animals. They write to say they're "still a happy family" with a long-term survivor.
"I sleep well at night getting those types of emails," Mamula said.
Dog owners should contact vet clinics directly to enroll in the clinical trials. A list of locations is available on the websites for TheraJan and the Canine Cancer Alliance.

【turn1039news34】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 8 months ago; A groundbreaking study led by the Wellcome Sanger Institute has revealed that domestic cats share significant genetic similarities with humans in the development of cancer, offering new avenues for treatment in both species. Researchers analyzed 13 types of feline tumors from nearly 500 cats across five countries by sequencing DNA from cancerous and healthy tissues. They found mutations in about 1,000 genes linked to human cancers, across various tumor types like blood, bone, lung, skin, gastrointestinal, and central nervous system cancers.

One key finding relates to feline breast cancer, where over half showed mutations in the FBXW7 gene—rare in humans but linked to worse outcomes. Tests with common chemotherapy drugs such as vincristine and vinorelbine successfully suppressed tumor growth in cat tissues with FBXW7 mutations. This discovery positions felines as potential early test subjects for treatments, especially where human clinical trials are harder to implement.

The research highlights the value of "comparative oncology," studying cancer across species, akin to research on elephants' resistance to tumors. Experts suggest these cross-species studies could offer vital insights into cancer prevention and treatment for humans.
